items.readable_text:
Content:
When analyzing data, we might have a data set of paired observations [MATH: (x_i, y_i)] in which the [MATH: y]-values increase or decrease rapidly as the [MATH: x]-values increase. In these situations, we might be able to fit the data to an exponential curve.

Content:
Consider the set of paired values [MATH: (x_i, y_i),] shown below.

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/1205551dc24af4a8abab76fb82dd37b5]

Content:
This data set certainly looks like it follows an exponential trend, but how can we be sure?

Content:
If the data is exponential, then the points should be scattered along a curve of the form

Content:
[MATH: y=a b^x,]
where [MATH: a > 0] (since the [MATH: y]-intercept of the trend-curve is positive) and [MATH: b > 1] (since the [MATH: y]-values are increasing).

Content:
If we take the logarithm to base [MATH: 10] on both sides of this equation, we get

Content:
[MATH: \log(y) = \log(ab^x).]

Content:
Applying the product rule for logarithms, we get

Content:
[MATH: \log(y) = \log(a) + \log(b^x).]

Content:
We then apply the power rule, which yields

Content:
[MATH: \log(y) =\log(a) + x\cdot \log(b) \qquad\qquad(\ast)]

Content:
Now, we define

Content:
[MATH: Y = \log(y), \qquad A = \log{a}, \qquad B = \log{b}.]

Content:
With these definitions, equation [MATH: (\ast)] becomes

Content:
[MATH: Y = A + Bx,]

Content:
which is a linear equation in the variables [MATH: x] and [MATH: Y.]

Content:
The key takeaway here is the following:

Content:
> When a data set [MATH: (x_i, y_i)] varies exponentially, the data set [MATH: (x_i, Y_i) = (x_i, \log(y_i))] varies linearly.

Content:
In this case, plotting [MATH: (x_i, Y_i)] for all pairs in our data set gives the following graph.

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/157b24c65e000ccc7cc268db960e8f4e]

Content:
This type of plot is called a semi-log scatter plot. Notice that the paired values [MATH: (x_i, Y_i)] follow a linear trend, which confirms that [MATH: (x_i, y_i)] follows an exponential trend.

sections.normalized_html:
We have an exponential decay model of the form [MATH: y=a \cdot b^x,] which means that [MATH: 0 < b < 1.]

To get the corresponding semi-log plot, we apply [MATH: \log] to both sides of [MATH: y = a \cdot b^x.] This gives

[MATH: y|= a ⋅ b^{x}; \log y|= \log (a ⋅ b^{x}); \log y|= \log a + \log b^{x}; \log y|= \log a + x ⋅ \log b; Y|= A + Bx,]

where

[MATH: Y=\log y,\qquad A=\log a,\qquad B=\log b.]

Now, since [MATH: 0< b < 1,] we obtain that [MATH: B=\log b < 0.] Therefore, the line [MATH: Y = A+Bx] must have a negative slope.

Content:
Earlier, we found the following semi-log scatter plot for a data set that followed a trend of the form [MATH: y = ab^x.]

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/6be42c149a030ee7f7405a6c3051e5a9]

Content:
The trend line equation for our semi-log scatter plot is

Content:
[MATH: Y = A + Bx,]
where

Content:
[MATH: Y=\log y,\qquad
A=\log a,\qquad
B=\log b.]

Content:
From here, we can deduce the following about the constants [MATH: a] and [MATH: b\mathbin{:}]

Content:
- Since the slope of the trend line is positive, we have [MATH: B > 0.] Therefore,
[MATH: b = 10^B > 1.]
This confirms that [MATH: y = ab^x] is an exponential growth curve.
- Since the [MATH: Y]-intercept of the trend line is positive, we have [MATH: A > 0.] Therefore,
[MATH: a = 10^A > 1.]

The semi-log scatter plot below represents a relationship of the form [MATH: y \approx a \cdot b^x] between the temperature [MATH: (y)] of an oven, in Celsius degrees, and the number of minutes [MATH: (x)] since the oven was turned off. Which of the following could be that relationship?

  1. [MATH: y \approx 3 \cdot 4^x]

  2. [MATH: y \approx 3 \cdot (0.4)^x]

sections.readable_text:

The semi-log scatter plot below represents a relationship of the form [MATH: y \approx a \cdot b^x] between the temperature [MATH: (y)] of an oven, in Celsius degrees, and the number of minutes [MATH: (x)] since the oven was turned off. Which of the following could be that relationship?

1. [MATH: y \approx 3 \cdot 4^x]
2. [MATH: y \approx 3 \cdot (0.4)^x]
3. [MATH: y \approx 0.3 \cdot 4^x]

sections.normalized_html: EXPLANATION
sections.readable_text: EXPLANATION

sections.normalized_html:
First, notice that the trend line [MATH: Y=A+Bx] corresponding to the data in our semi-log scatter plot

  • has a negative slope, meaning that [MATH: B < 0,] and

  • has a positive [MATH: Y]-intercept, meaning that [MATH: A >0.]

To get the corresponding semi-log plot for [MATH: y = a \cdot b^x], we apply [MATH: \log] to both sides of the equation and get

[MATH: y|= a ⋅ b^{x}; \log y|= \log (a ⋅ b^{x}); \log y|= \log a + \log b^{x}; \log y|= \log a + x ⋅ \log b; Y|= A + Bx,]

where

[MATH: Y=\log y,\qquad A=\log a,\qquad B=\log b.]

As a result, we have

[MATH: B|< 0; \log b|< 0; 0 < b|< 1]

and

[MATH: A|> 0; \log a|> 0; a|> 1.]

Among the given options, the only exponential model that fits the description is

[MATH: y \approx 3 \cdot (0.4)^x.]

Item 1 — Tutorial: Introduction

Content:

Content:
Consider the set of paired values [MATH: (x_i, y_i),] shown below.

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/1205551dc24af4a8abab76fb82dd37b5]

Content:
This data set certainly looks like it follows an exponential trend, but how can we be sure?

Content:
If the data is exponential, then the points should be scattered along a curve of the form

Content:
[MATH: y=a b^x,]
where [MATH: a > 0] (since the [MATH: y]-intercept of the trend-curve is positive) and [MATH: b > 1] (since the [MATH: y]-values are increasing).

Content:
If we take the logarithm to base [MATH: 10] on both sides of this equation, we get

Content:
[MATH: \log(y) = \log(ab^x).]

Content:
Applying the product rule for logarithms, we get

Content:
[MATH: \log(y) = \log(a) + \log(b^x).]

Content:
We then apply the power rule, which yields

Content:
[MATH: \log(y) =\log(a) + x\cdot \log(b) \qquad\qquad(\ast)]

Content:
Now, we define

Content:
[MATH: Y = \log(y), \qquad A = \log{a}, \qquad B = \log{b}.]

Content:
With these definitions, equation [MATH: (\ast)] becomes

Content:
[MATH: Y = A + Bx,]

Content:
which is a linear equation in the variables [MATH: x] and [MATH: Y.]

Content:
The key takeaway here is the following:

Content:
> When a data set [MATH: (x_i, y_i)] varies exponentially, the data set [MATH: (x_i, Y_i) = (x_i, \log(y_i))] varies linearly.

Content:
In this case, plotting [MATH: (x_i, Y_i)] for all pairs in our data set gives the following graph.

EXPLANATION

Explanation:
We have an exponential decay model of the form [MATH: y=a \cdot b^x,] which means that [MATH: 0 < b < 1.]

To get the corresponding semi-log plot, we apply [MATH: \log] to both sides of [MATH: y = a \cdot b^x.] This gives

[MATH: y|= a ⋅ b^{x}; \log y|= \log (a ⋅ b^{x}); \log y|= \log a + \log b^{x}; \log y|= \log a + x ⋅ \log b; Y|= A + Bx,]

where

[MATH: Y=\log y,\qquad
A=\log a,\qquad
B=\log b.]

Now, since [MATH: 0< b < 1,] we obtain that
[MATH: B=\log b < 0.]
Therefore, the line [MATH: Y = A+Bx] must have a negative slope.

Item 5 — Tutorial: Making Inferences From a Semi-Log Scatter Plot

Content:
Earlier, we found the following semi-log scatter plot for a data set that followed a trend of the form [MATH: y = ab^x.]

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/6be42c149a030ee7f7405a6c3051e5a9]

Content:
The trend line equation for our semi-log scatter plot is

Content:
[MATH: Y = A + Bx,]
where

Content:
[MATH: Y=\log y,\qquad
A=\log a,\qquad
B=\log b.]

Content:
From here, we can deduce the following about the constants [MATH: a] and [MATH: b\mathbin{:}]

Content:
- Since the slope of the trend line is positive, we have [MATH: B > 0.] Therefore,
[MATH: b = 10^B > 1.]
This confirms that [MATH: y = ab^x] is an exponential growth curve.
- Since the [MATH: Y]-intercept of the trend line is positive, we have [MATH: A > 0.] Therefore,
[MATH: a = 10^A > 1.]

Item 6 — Example: Identifying an Exponential Model Corresponding to a Semi-Log Scatter Plot

Example Prompt:
[IMG: /graphics/9f16ab9e25e90667ed4ad6badd25c052]

The semi-log scatter plot below represents a relationship of the form [MATH: y \approx a \cdot b^x] between the temperature [MATH: (y)] of an oven, in Celsius degrees, and the number of minutes [MATH: (x)] since the oven was turned off. Which of the following could be that relationship?

1. [MATH: y \approx 3 \cdot 4^x]
2. [MATH: y \approx 3 \cdot (0.4)^x]
3. [MATH: y \approx 0.3 \cdot 4^x]

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
First, notice that the trend line [MATH: Y=A+Bx] corresponding to the data in our semi-log scatter plot

- has a negative slope, meaning that [MATH: B < 0,] and
- has a positive [MATH: Y]-intercept, meaning that [MATH: A >0.]

To get the corresponding semi-log plot for [MATH: y = a \cdot b^x], we apply [MATH: \log] to both sides of the equation and get

[MATH: y|= a ⋅ b^{x}; \log y|= \log (a ⋅ b^{x}); \log y|= \log a + \log b^{x}; \log y|= \log a + x ⋅ \log b; Y|= A + Bx,]

where

[MATH: Y=\log y,\qquad
A=\log a,\qquad
B=\log b.]

As a result, we have

[MATH: B|< 0; \log b|< 0; 0 < b|< 1]

and

[MATH: A|> 0; \log a|> 0; a|> 1.]

Among the given options, the only exponential model that fits the description is

[MATH: y \approx 3 \cdot (0.4)^x.]
